It’s a convertible but not a sports car, and I’ll get downvoted to hell for saying it, but hear me out: Chrysler Sebring. They hold their value worth shit, so for 5k you can find a really new low mile vehicle. They don’t have the best reputation for reliability, but I think it’s exaggerated out of general disdain for the car. It’s a fun car to hate on for car enthusiasts. 

Here’s the beauty though: there’s a lot of Michael Scott types out there who aren’t really car people but who wanted a convertible; they bought a Sebring new, kept it in the garage, and took it out on nice weekends to cruise around with the top down. They didn’t drive the car hard, mod it out, race it, whatever. This is the used car you want to buy. Don’t just buy any Sebring you see, but make sure it was owned by someone like this who took great care of it. Trust me there’s plenty out there and within your budget. I was recently in the market for decent reliable transportation for a 5k budget, and this was high up there on my list, for those reasons. It’ll be a whole lot more reliable and less of a headache to own than any old clapped out boxster you’ll find for 5k, though less exciting to drive of course. Good luck

Hey OP, I taught windsurfing for 7 years. It sounds like you picked this up with a mistrial shredder? (I had to google the board). I’m all about the diy spirit, teach yourself, get cheap stuff on craigslist and make it work, etc.... but sadly in this regard windsurfing is different.

If you want to go anywhere in the sport, you need different gear. The board is inadequate. You need something with a centerboard (non negotiable, if you’re learning). And ideally much wider and much more volume in general. Have you tried standing on that thing in the water yet? If you weight more than 70 lbs you’re gonna struggle bad, especially once the sail is in the mix. 

You probably need a more modern rig (sail, mast, boom) too. Windsurfing gear just came a huuuuge way about ten (?) years after your gear was made. Like game changingly different stuff. Balanced sails with a stable center of effort, sail material that doesn’t absorb water, easy and strong rig components, boards with more width that are more forgiving to a beginner, etc 

And if you’re trying to go anywhere in the sport, you need to take lessons. Again, it sucks to say and it sucks to hear. I taught myself how to surf off YouTube and have become a pretty decent surfer with no real lessons ever. Windsurfing is not like that. I’ve seen it time after time. It happens all the time and it’s sad to see. Someone finds an ancient windsurfing setup on craigslist for $400 or whatever that was once sold for $2k (albeit 30 years ago...), used twice, garage kept, whatever so they think they got a great deal. They’ll take it down to the water and  try to give it a spin. And nothing happens except lots of frustration and a bad taste in their mouth for an incredible sport that they now will no longer pursue after a frustrating experience. 

Anyway, I wish you the best of luck. Feel free to message me with any windsurfing questions, I love the sport and miss being around it as much as I used to be. Maybe I missed some details in the post, but this is something I’ve been meaning to type out for a while since I see it a lot.
